summary: This work demonstrates that detector error model (DEM) event probabilities for surface-code decoders can be estimated directly from experimental syndrome data without separate calibration or device benchmarking. Syndrome-estimated DEMs reduce logical error probabilities by 5%–10% relative to baseline device-informed DEMs on both Google's Willow chip (rotated ZXXZ surface code with $d\in\{3,5,7\}$) and IBM's ibm_miami processor (unrotated code with $d=3$), reaching ~38% improvement in single-cycle cases on IBM without requiring additional circuits or supervised fitting.
motivation: Standard DEM characterization methods such as tomography do not scale to large QEC systems, and prior Pauli noise-learning approaches require extra pre-optimization circuits. Recent theoretical work suggested syndrome-based DEM estimation is feasible, but decoder-level logical performance across multiple devices, distances, and cycle counts remained unexplored.
method: DEM event probabilities on fixed reference detector-logical supports are estimated from empirical detector moments and covariances computed over 50,000 experimental shots per case, using hierarchical inversion formulas for graphlike and hyperedge rates (equations 17–26). Logical error probabilities are then evaluated by decoding experimental syndromes with MWPM using these estimated DEMs, compared against SI1000 circuit-level and RL-optimized baseline DEMs.
result: For Willow across nine subsystems and $d\in\{3,5,7\}$ with $r\in\{1,10,13,30,50,70\}$ cycles, syndrome-estimated DEMs yield $\Delta P_L$ values typically $\lesssim -10\%$ relative to SI1000 and perform comparably to RL-optimized DEMs; for ibm_miami at $d=3$ with $r\leq19$ cycles, syndrome-estimated DEMs reduce logical error probabilities 5%–10% relative to IBM-like baseline, with larger gains when dynamical decoupling eliminates coherent errors and negative detector covariances.
